   1|                                                                              In Memoriam
   2|                        Marion M. Benson, 83
   3|                        Marion passed away on December 27, 2015 in Leominster. She was very active in the Town of
   4|                        Lunenburg where she lived for 40 plus years. She was an active volunteer in both church & civic
   5|                       groups, including the School Committee. After her return to Lunenburg in 1981, she began
   6|                       volunteering on the Planning Board, where she quickly became Chairperson. She volunteered for
   7|                       two decades on the Board at which time the position evolved into full-time Planning Director; a
   8|                       position she held until 2014. In May 2015, her many years of service were recognized at Annual
   9|                       Town Meeting by a Ritter Building conference room being named in her honor.
  10|                                             August "Gus" S. Misner, 78
  11|                                             Gus passed away on July 15, 2015 in Togus, Maine following a long battle with cancer.
  12|                                            He was born in Fitchburg on December 17, 1936 where he attended school and played
  13|                                            football. He served in the U.S. Army from 1955-1964, was stationed in the Arctic and was
  14|                                            an aide to President Eisenhower. He later became a police officer in Lunenburg for several
  15|                                             years until ill health forced his retirement.
  16|                                         Senator Mary Padula, 89
  17|                              Mary Louise Padula, nee Harley, passed away on October 29, 2015. Born in Fitchburg and
  18|                              nearly a lifetime resident of Lunenburg, Mary served as Town Clerk, Tax Collector and
  19|                              Treasurer for 30 years. Upon leaving the Town Hall, she represented the Second Worcester
  20|                              and Middlesex District in the Massachusetts Senate for 8 years, and as part of Governor
  21|                              Weld's cabinet, served as Secretary of Housing & Community Development for 5 years.
  22|                              She served as President of the Massachusetts Treasurer and Tax Collector Association and
  23|                              as Assistant Minority Leader in the Senate and on many boards and committees. She was
  24|                             recognized by Fitchburg State College as one of the 100 citizens who made the greatest
  25|                             difference in North Central Massachusetts in the last 100 years.
  26|                                                David M. Shea, 67
  27|                                                David Shea passed away on August 8, 2015 after a courageous battle with cancer. David
  28|                                                was an atmospheric scientist with an environmental consulting company for 37 years.
  29|                                                He was a longtime resident of Lunenburg. David was an original founder of the
  30|                                                Lunenburg Recycling Commission and a member of the Board of Health for 30 years.
  31|                                                He was a passionate golfer who enjoyed playing as well as organizing an annual golf
  32|                                                tournament. David was a soccer coach and a high school soccer referee for many years.
  33|                                                David was known for his great sense of humor and his unending energy. He seemed to
  34|                                                know everyone and was referred to many times as the "Mayor of Lunenburg."
  35|                                                                                                      3

   1|                                                                                     LUNENBURG
   2|                       Lunenburg          was settled in 1718 and incorporated in 1728. It occupies a land area of
   3|                       approximately 26.4 square miles. Lunenburg is located in north central Massachusetts
   4|                       approximately 43 miles from Boston. It is bordered on the west by the Town of Ashby and the
   5|                       City of Fitchburg, on the south by the Town of Lancaster and the City of Leominster, on the east
   6|                       by the Town of Shirley, and on the north by the Town of Townsend.
   7|                        Local legislative decisions are made by an open town meeting consisting of all registered voters
   8|                       in the town. Subject to the legislative decisions made by town meeting, the affairs of the town
   9|                       are generally administered by a five member Board of Selectmen and a Town Manager. Local
  10|                       school affairs are administered by an elected seven member School Committee while local taxes
  11|                       are assessed by a three member Board of Assessors, all are appointed on an at-large basis for
  12|                       staggered three-year terms.
  13|                       Lunenburg is a semi-rural community located in northern Worcester County. Three water bodies
  14|                       account for somewhat of a clustered approach to the town's historical development. Lake
  15|                       Whalom and the former Whalom Amusement Park delineated the Whalom District from the
  16|                       remainder of Lunenburg. This district was developed as a housing base for many factory
  17|                       workers working in the mills and factories of Leominster and Fitchburg. In many ways the
  18|                       characteristics of the Whalom District more closely reflect characteristics of these cities than of
  19|                       the rest of Lunenburg. The Hickory Hills area of town, around Hickory Hills Lake, was
  20|                       developed as a private community comprised largely of vacation cottages. The third body of
  21|                       water is Shirley Reservoir, a public water body also developed with mainly vacation cottages
  22|                       that have now been modified to year-round residences. Commercial and industrial development
  23|                       is permitted in several areas of town, primarily along the two major arteries (Routes 2A and 13),
  24|                       and the town's peripheries, due largely to the close proximity of Leominster's and Fitchburg's
  25|                       sewer and water systems. Although many farms and orchards had slowly developed into single
  26|                       family housing, farming continues on in Lunenburg. At the Annual Town Meeting on May 4*
  27|                       2013, the Town voted to establish an Agricultural Commission to represent, preserve, and
  28|                       enhance farming in the community and to administer the "Right to Farm" bylaw.
  29|                                                 Lunenburg Centre, Lunenburg, Mass.

===PAGE 19=== (ocr, 50 lines)
   1|                                                                    REPORT OF THE TOWN MANAGER
   2|                        The Town continued to make important progress in 2015 in many areas, including: School Building;
   3|                         Building Reuse; Increased Public Transportation; and updating the Pavement Management Plan. The MS/
   4|                        HS building is well under construction and set to open in September 2016. Fifty-eight (58%) of the
   5|                        project's eligible costs will be paid through a grant from the MA School Building Authority. As of
   6|                         December 31, 2015, approximately $30M of the Town's total share had been permanently financed in order
   7|                        to take best advantage of the low interest rates.
   8|                        The Board of Selectmen (BOS) appointed Building Reuse Committee continued its work throughout 2015.
   9|                        In the summer, the Committee issued a Request for Proposals for a Building Reuse and Space Needs Study.
  10|                        Town's goal for the Project was to assess the existing conditions of four (4) buildings owned by the Town
  11|                        and determine the most cost effective building(s) to accommodate the Town's current and anticipated space
  12|                        needs for Town administrative operations currently housed at Town Hall and remote sites. The building(s)
  13|                        that are determined not to be advantageous to the Town may be deemed as "surplus property" and disposed
  14|                        of in accordance with M.G.L. c. 30B§16. The Assessment and Space Needs study include the following
  15|                        four (4) buildings: Town Hall; Ritter Memorial Building: Thomas C. Passios Elementary; and the Brooks
  16|                        House. In late summer, the Town hired Tappé & Associates, the same firm serving as Architect on the MS/
  17|                        HS School Project, to complete this study. The results of the study were presented to the BOS in 2016.
  18|                        The BOS worked diligently with the Department of Public Works to update its existing Pavement
  19|                        Management Plan. The updated plan built upon the foundation of the existing plan but included additional
  20|                        evaluation criteria. The original plan was developed in 2009 and funding decisions from that point up until
  21|                        FY16 were based upon that plan. Beginning in FY2017, all funding decisions will be based upon the
  22|                        revised plan which established a PCI, or Pavement Condition Index, for each roadway and a Prioritize List
  23|                        which takes into account both the functional classification of the roadway and the needed repair. The
  24|                        Board further determined that a PCI of 70 would be considered a generally acceptable pavement condition
  25|                        and worked on determining the best funding mechanism for the PMP Program to insure that maintenance
  26|                        needs would be addressed uniformly across all roadway classifications. To that end, the Board agreed to
  27|                        put forth a debt exemption question to the voters, seeking an additional $4M in tax dollars to complete the
  28|                        large backlog of needed maintenance & repair work. The work would be completed over a period of 3 - 4
  29|                        years and would be financed over a period of at least twice as long. Thereafter, the Town would endeavor
  30|                        to include additional funding within the Operating Budget to provide for a sufficient level of funding to
  31|                        maintain roads at a PCI of 70.
  32|                         The Town also continued to work on its largest and most comprehensive roadway project, the
  33|                        redevelopment of Summer Street, a project slated to begin in fall of 2016. In 2014, the Town committed
  34|                        $230,312 from Chapter 90 Funding to fund the Town's portion of the 75% design. The project is expected
  35|                        to cost about $7M, all of which will be funded though the Regional Transportation Improvement Plan
  36|                        (TIP), which is a grant of State & Federal funds. The project was approved for TIP funding for FFY2017.
  37|                         One of the most exciting projects which continued into 2015 was the implementation of enhanced public
  38|                        transportation within Lunenburg. The Town pays both an annual assessment to the MART and to the
  39|                         MBTA. The assessment to MART pays for local/ regional transportation. The assessment to the MBTA
  40|                        pays for access to the commuter rail system in Fitchburg and Leominster. The Town learned through
  41|                        MART that there is a provision in State Law that would allow the Town to use its MBTA Assessment to
  42|                        purchase additional local transportation, at no additional cost to the taxpayer. Accordingly, the Town
  43|                        undertook a review of residents' transportation needs and began working with MART to provide additional
  44|                        local transportation. The additional services began in spring 2015, though ridership was low. The Town
  45|                        was able to revise its transportation offerings to include limited service along the full length of Route 2A,
  46|                        from the town center to the Shirley line. The Town will continue to monitor ridership and make
  47|                        adjustments as needed to best service the public.
  48|                        I would be remiss if I did not take this opportunity to thank all of the people in this town who give of their
  49|                        time and many talents to make Lunenburg a better place. Thank you all for your dedicated service.
  50|                                                                                                     19

   1|                                                                                BOARD OF ASSESSORS
   2|                        The Board of Assessors saw its first transition in a number of years. Elected to the Board twenty-one years ago,
   3|                       Christopher Comeau chose not to seek re-election. Chris was a reliable and respected member who could be
   4|                       counted on to support the office in its long-standing mission to improve the office, render fair tax assessments, and
   5|                       treat the taxpaying public well. Never shying away from offering opinions over the Town's financial state, he
   6|                       sought to find balance between financial prudence and supporting worthwhile projects.
   7|                        Replacing Mr. Comeau on the Board is Richard Letarte, a prominent accountant and businessman. Mr. Letarte
   8|                       brings considerable experience and time to work on special assignments.
   9|                       The Assessors' administrative staff, Louise Paquette and Sheila Craigen, along with the professional assessment
  10|                       staff of Regional Resource Group, Inc. (RRG) led by Harald Scheid round out the office. RRG veteran assessor
  11|                       Rebecca Boucher replaced George Bourgault as Associate Regional Assessor.
  12|                       The office anticipates a busy 2016 calendar year. An improving economy will see the construction of more homes
  13|                        and apartment dwellings.

   1|                                                                                 Agricultural Commission
   2|                                   The Agricultural Commission was created in 2013 with the aim of encouraging the continued
   3|                       pursuit of agriculture in Lunenburg, promoting agriculturally-based economic opportunities, providing an
   4|                       opportunity for mediation and negotiation of farming issues, educating the community and advocating for
   5|                       the continued understanding of the importance of locally produced food and farm products.
   6|                                   With this continued understanding and the continued support of the community, we can work
   7|                       toward the preservation of prime agricultural lands, which serve to beautify Lunenburg visually and
   8|                       maintain the rural charm wherein Lunenburg's appeal lies.
   9|                                  The Agricultural Commission has had the opportunity to mediate several issues concerning
  10|                       farming and has tried through education and investigation to help the parties involved reach equitable
  11|                       arrangements within the existing laws and protections.
  12|                                   We have provided information to prospective buyers of agricultural property in town as well as
  13|                       providing guidance to residents preparing to go before town commissions. We are currently adding links
  14|                       to information and services from the Agricultural Commission website. With the strong support of the
  15|                       Board of Selectmen, the Agricultural Commission was able to substantially expand the Lunenburg
  16|                       Community Farmers' Market, offering a wider variety of vendors, products and musical entertainment
  17|                       from the local area.
  18|                                   The Agricultural Commission would like to express heartfelt thanks to the Farmers' Market site
  19|                       management team, to the participating vendors, the entertainers (usually paid in produce!) and especially
  20|                       to the members of the community who have shown a strong and consistent support of the market and the
  21|                       local farmers who depend on community patronage.
  22|                       The Agricultural Commission is:
  23|                       Jeffrey L. Mendoza, Chairman,
  24|                       Garrett Stillman, Vice-Chairman
  25|                       Maureen Dupuis, Clerk
  26|                       Douglas MacMillan, Member
  27|                       Renee Trakimas, Member
  28|                       The Commission would also like to express tremendous gratitude to our Planning Board liaison, Mr.
  29|                       Matthew Allison for his tireless work in providing maps, regulations, bylaw references and research to the
  30|                       Agricultural Commission.
  31|                       Thank you to the Town of Lunenburg for your continued support of the Agricultural Commission and its
  32|                       mission toward preserving the agricultural fabric of our town.
  33|                       Respectfully Submitted,
  34|                       Jeffrey L. Mendoza, Chairman
  35|                       Lunenburg Agricultural Commission
  36|                                                                                                     49

===PAGE 50=== (ocr, 31 lines)
   1|                                                                               BUILDING DEPARTMENT
   2|                       The Building Department is located on the second floor of the Ritter Memorial Building, 960 Massachusetts
   3|                       Avenue, Lunenburg, MA. Office hours for the Building Department are Monday and Wednesday 8:00 A.M. to
   4|                       4:00 P.M., Tuesday and Thursday 8:00 A.M. to 6:00 P.M. The Building Department is closed on Fridays.
   5|                       Michael J. Sauvageau serves as the Building Commissioner, John Morreale serves as the Assistant Building
   6|                       Inspector and Lisa Normandin is the department Administrative Assistant.
   7|                       The Building Department now processes all Wiring, Plumbing and Gas permits, a duty that was formerly done in
   8|                       the Office of the Town Clerk.
   9|                       Building permits for 2015 decreased slightly from 481 in 2014 to 452 for 2015 but still reflects increased
  10|                       construction activity since the tail end of the economic and housing downturn a couple of years back. Solar
  11|                       permits remain steady as does new single family homes and townhouses. The Emerald Place project should be
  12|                       completed this year. Several large projects are in the reviewing stage or have been approved and are anticipated to
  13|                       begin construction soon. The new high school is progressing well and it appears it will be completed on or before
  14|                       The 2009 International Building Code for residential and commercial construction is the current building code
  15|                       and it is anticipated that a new Ninth Edition Code (2015 International Building Code) will be in effect by June of
  16|                       this year.
  17|                       Residents and developers are reminded that Lunenburg is a "Stretch Code Community" which has specific
  18|                       code requirements in addition to the current energy code requirements.
  19|                        Carbon monoxide detectors are required by law to be installed in every home regardless of the age of the
  20|                       dwelling. Also, all swimming pools are required to obtain a building permit and an electrical permit. Inflatable
  21|                       pools that do not have code required fencing around them do not meet the building code and should be removed.
  22|                       Residents should be aware that inflatable swimming pools do not meet code compliance requirements. Please
  23|                       contact our office to determine what steps need to take place for compliance and safety.
  24|                       Residents should be aware that Massachusetts Law requires that all persons, partnerships and corporations who
  25|                       bid or perform residential contracting (reconstruction, alterations, additions etc.) for work exceeding $1000.00 be
  26|                       registered with the Commonwealth. This office will enforce this provision, however you should ask your
  27|                       contractor about his/her registration. Please contact this office with any questions about this requirement or call
  28|                       for any information regarding zoning requirements or building code issues.
  29|                       Michael J. Sauvageau
  30|                       Building Commissioner & Zoning Official

   1|                                                                    Conservation Commission
   2|                       The Town of Lunenburg Conservation Commission is a seven member board appointed to 3-year terms
   3|                       by the Board of Selectmen, whose duties are codified under the Conservation Commission Act M.G.L.
   4|                       Chapter 40, § &C. The Commission enforces the Massachusetts Wetland Protection Act M.G.L. Chapter
   5|                       131, 840 and Article XXII of the local bylaws for the protection of wetlands.
   6|                       The year 2015 was one of a very busy and active agenda containing both public hearings and meetings for
   7|                       a wide range of projects from commercial development, subdivisions and small single family upkeep
   8|                       projects. The Conservation Commission worked to spell out goals of preparing to use the year 2016 to
   9|                       revise its regulations to provide consistency with the original by-law and to find those sections that may
  10|                       be out of date and need to be modified.
  11|                       The Commission held numerous inspections with its agent on weekends prior to meetings to familiarize
  12|                       themselves with the upcoming proposals that would appear on their agenda. The Commission is working
  13|                       with the Town on familiarizing itself with the upcoming storm water mandates from the EPA and
  14|                       working towards compliance both by procedure and with any necessary codification.
  15|                       The Conservation Commission in cooperation with the Open Space Committee and the Lunenburg Snow
  16|                       Riders Club has closed out a grant that obtained the former Lane property as Open Space and has worked
  17|                       to place an adequate and American Disabilities Act- compliant parking area that would blend in with the
  18|                       trail heads on Holman Street. The Snow Riders continue to obtain grant monies to continue to improve
  19|                       trail access to be enjoyed by all. The Conservation Commission held public recreational walks through its
  20|                       open space parcels and plans to continue to do so.
  21|                       This year also marked the retirement of Janice Carrier, who worked diligently with the Conservation
  22|                       Commission as the Administrator for the past 10 years. The Commission would like to take this
  23|                       opportunity to thank her for her tremendous efforts and wishes her a healthy and happy retirement!
  24|                       Currently Consulting Agent Matthew S. Marro is manning the office in both capacities taking Janice's
  25|                       place. But no one will ever fill her shoes!
  26|                       The Commission thanks all the town agencies for a great year and looks forward to many more!
  27|                       Respectfully Submitted,
  28|                       Richard Bursch, Chair
  29|                       Jack Rabbitt, Vice-Chair
  30|                       Brad Kennedy
  31|                       Tom Bertram
  32|                       Carl Luck
  33|                       Todd Dwyer
  34|                       Kenneth Jones
  35|                       Matthew S. Marro, Agent

   1|                                                                                 COUNCIL ON AGING
   2|                       The mission of the Council on Aging is to advocate for the improved quality of life for all seniors through
   3|                       supportive services, programs and education. Councils on Aging were established under Massachusetts
   4|                       General Law Chapter 40, § 8B, to include setting policy for the administration of elder programs or
   5|                       services and to develop, coordinate and conduct such activities which advocate for elder issues.
   6|                       The FY15 Council on Aging staff consisted of Doreen C. Noble, Director; Susan Doherty, Administrative
   7|                        Assistant and Transportation; Faith A. Anderson, Outreach Coordinator; Joanne Brazell, Ruth Swiecicki,
   8|                       and Jeanne Tatro, Meal Site Coordinators; Judy Alario and Elsa Watson, Meal Site Assistants; Gerry
   9|                       Beloin and Jim McGuigan, MART Van Drivers.
  10|                       The Council on Aging Board is an eleven member board appointed by the Lunenburg Board of
  11|                       Selectmen.
  12|                       The FY15 Council on Aging Board members were; Chairperson Pete Lincoln, Vice-Chairperson Deb
  13|                       Seeley, Betty DiGiacomo, Jacquelyn Dwyer, Sarah Grant, Brian Guenard, Deb Lincoln, Kevin McNally,
  14|                       Cheryl Moisan, Diane Nowd, and Judith Tarbell.
  15|                       The Town budget alone does not support this senior center. Other sources of funding are the Eagle House
  16|                       Supporters Inc., a non-profit 501(c)3 group, Formula Grant funding from the Commonwealth of
  17|                       Massachusetts, and Montachusett Regional Transit Authority.
  18|                       We are very lucky to have a large volunteer force at the Eagle House. In FY15 we had 41 volunteers who
  19|                       contributed 2,587.25 hours of their time to help us out by doing things such as driving for the Meals on
  20|                       Wheels Program, program leaders, kitchen helpers, office help, library, and friendly visitors. We greatly
  21|                       appreciate their service.
  22|                       The Eagle House offered a variety of programs, such as health and wellness, arts and crafts,
  23|                       intergenerational, cards and games, cultural, information and referral, and social events both at the senior
  24|                       center and offsite.
  25|                       In FY15 the Council on Aging delivered 4898 Meals on Wheels to 50 clients and provided 3,169 rides to
  26|                       62 clients on our senior van. Our combined events and service statistics totaled 10,060 units with 827
  27|                       participants.
  28|                                                                                                     53

===PAGE 54=== (ocr, 17 lines)
   1|                                                                    LUNENBURG CULTURAL COUNCIL
   2|                                                                                       (Fiscal Year 2015)
   3|                       The Lunenburg Cultural Council is part of a network of 329 Local Cultural Councils serving all
   4|                        351 cities and towns in the Commonwealth. The LCC Program is the largest grassroots cultural
   5|                       funding network in the nation, supporting thousands of community-based projects in the arts,
   6|                        sciences and humanities every year. The state legislature provides an annual appropriation to the
   7|                        Massachusetts Cultural Council, a state agency, which then allocates funds to each community.
   8|                       The Lunenburg Cultural Council received and will distribute $4,300 in grants. These funds are
   9|                       granted to qualified individuals and organizations to support cultural projects that benefit the
  10|                        community. These grants can support a variety of artistic projects and activities in Lunenburg
  11|                       including exhibits, festivals, field trips, short-term artist residencies or performances in schools,
  12|                        workshops and lectures.
  13|                       The LCC met December 3, 2014 at the Lunenburg Public Library to decide grant distribution for
  14|                       this year's cycle (2015). All rejection and acceptance letters were mailed by December 30th.
  15|                        Applications for FY'2016 were due by October 15, 2015.
  16|                       More information about the Local Cultural Council Program is available online at
  17|                       http://www.mass-culture.org/lcc_public.aspx.

   1|                                                                       DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
   2|                                    The Department of Public Works combines the resources of the Highway, Park, Cemetery,
   3|                       Sewer, and Facilities divisions, and Vehicle Maintenance services into one department organizing and
   4|                       scheduling personnel and equipment to best serve the residents of the community through the effective
   5|                       delivery of an extensive scope of services with a high degree of efficiency.
   6|                       DEPARTMENTAL OBJECTIVES
   7|                                   "Public Works is either working or on call twenty four hours a day three hundred and sixty five
   8|                       days a year to respond to any weather, infrastructure, roadway, or facility related emergency that may
   9|                                    We strive to enhance the awareness of the value of Public Works provides to our Town, and
  10|                        ensure others are aware of our contribution. This is not for an expectation of praise, but rather to make
  11|                       sure efforts are not forgotten as they merge into the fabric of our everyday service.
  12|                                    Major events over the past years have highlighted the fact that Public Works has a seat at the
  13|                       table and is a major player in emergency management. Town Officials, Police, and Fire acknowledge that
  14|                       Public Works is critical in order to facilitate the required services of others. We must continue to build on
  15|                        this awareness.
  16|                                    This department must also reach out to the public we serve and educate them to the fact that the
  17|                       common services they receive do not just happen, but rather are the efforts of a dedicated staff of
  18|                       individuals, service companies, and vendors. Safe roadways, wastewater control, solid waste collection
  19|                       and recycling operations, tree removal, storm water management facilities and grounds maintenance,
  20|                       winter snow and ice removal, cemeteries and parks are the expected services supporting everyone in the
  21|                       community.
  22|                                    We will work to engage the public in order to set reasonable expectations and gather support for
  23|                       annual budget requests, capital requests, and specific projects.
  24|                       PAVEMENT MANAGEMENT
  25|                                    The updated Pavement Management Plan, inclusive of an electronic database and a revised
  26|                        Town-wide pavement defect analysis. For a second time, a complete survey of every road was completed.
  27|                       The amount of new paving does not keep up with the seasonal deterioration factor, and as such the
  28|                       backlog in excess of nine million dollars. The program remains underfunded.
  29|                                    Road Projects typically extend over two construction seasons and overlap from one fiscal year to
  30|                       the next. During this year the following roads were addressed either totally or in part: Howard St.,
  31|                       Reservoir Rd., Goodrich St., and smaller sections of Arbor, Page, and Kilburn Sts.
  32|                                    Documentation provided through a "pot hole" log ( a daily record of road work specific to
  33|                       patching and filling of pot holes) proved that one third of all the available work days during the season are
  34|                       dedicated to patching and other temporary repairs to similar roadway failures. As defects are identified we
  35|                       respond to every location in a timely manner. This has proven to be as less than effective method of road
  36|                       repair. New pot holes appear each spring particularly after a severe winter, and often staff addresses the
  37|                        same areas year after year.
  38|                                   The seasonal crack sealing program has been effective in some locations however this application
  39|                       is designed as a temporary solution with an effective life span of around five years. Many streets that have
  40|                       been "sealed" are well beyond that time frame. This process involves the installation of rubberized asphalt
  41|                       under high pressure to cracks or separations in the pavement. The Pavement Management Plan identifies
  42|                       specific areas where this method is the best option. This application does not take the place of curb to
  43|                       curb paving, only postpones it and is not applicable in areas of more serious defects.
  44|                       The revised Pavement plan, no matter how detailed, is of little value without an identified source of
  45|                       funding. Lack of revenue continues to be the major detriment to improving the overall condition of our
  46|                                                                                                     55

===PAGE 56=== (ocr, 45 lines)
   1|                                   roadways. The primary sources of funding are the Massachusetts Department of Transportation
   2|                       Chapter 90 program and a dedicated line in the DPW budget. The estimated value of our 86 miles of
   3|                       paved streets is, by industry standards, calculated to be 62 million dollars. The General Highway
   4|                       maintenance line within the operational budget has remained virtually unchanged for two decades while
   5|                       the overall omnibus budget has nearly tripled to a value in excess of 30 million dollars. In order to initiate
   6|                        and sustain a road improvement program a substantial infusion of funds is necessary. The conservative
   7|                       estimate remains at approximately 1.2 million dollars per year total or an additional $800,000.00 to
   8|                       existing allocations. Applying $400,000-$500,000 a year to a backlog of work that approaches 10 million
   9|                       dollars dooms the current plan to failure. As an example: many roads are compromised to the degree that
  10|                       only a major reconstruction can bring them to an acceptable quality and less travelled, local roads remain
  11|                       out of reach.
  12|                       FLEET MAINTENANCE
  13|                                    The DPW is responsible for the repairs and preventative maintenance to all Town vehicles and
  14|                       equipment. High performance police units, First responder Fire and Rescue apparatus, park, cemetery,
  15|                       and school vehicles as well as over 30 pieces of highway related machinery are serviced by department
  16|                       personnel. Outsourcing of highly technical repairs has become more frequent and therefore more costly.
  17|                       Due to the volatile global oil market, the overall cost of fuel and petroleum based products continues to be
  18|                       a moving target and therefore difficult to estimate annually.
  19|                                    The installation of a vehicle maintenance software program has proven to be a valuable tool. Each
  20|                       repair is logged by department and vehicle identification number and memorialized in a data bank. Every
  21|                       vehicle can be tracked for part numbers, required services, as well as frequency and cost of repairs over
  22|                       the life of the equipment.

  36|                              Staff keeps buildings compliant and protects the safe running of the work environment. Any

===PAGE 57=== (ocr, 43 lines)
   1|                       ENVIRONMENTAL
   2|                       Storm Water
   3|                                    For yet another year the Environmental Protection Agency has not set the requirements for the
   4|                       next phase of storm water regulation and permits. As we await the potential of what will be an unfunded
   5|                        Federal mandate the Town remains in compliance with current protocol.
   6|                                    The DPW, as a result of limited funding is forced to become reactionary to roadway drainage
   7|                       issues. A capital program in the 1990's earmarked $20,000.00 annually toward rehabilitation/installation
   8|                       of piping and catch basins. The elimination of this dedicated funding placed the financial burden upon the
   9|                       overall General Highway maintenance allocation effectively reducing drainage repairs. In anticipation of
  10|                       the new regulations the Town Manager has re-established a budget line within the DPW dedicated to
  11|                        storm water, a necessary first step.
  12|                                    As roadways are scheduled for pavement, drainage is surveyed and necessary repairs are
  13|                       addressed. Little or no preventative maintenance, short of public safety issues in the form of flooding or
  14|                       structural failure, street sweeping and catch basin cleaning can be initiated due to a lack of available
  15|                       resources and the absences of a Town wide drainage survey. New storm water regulations will likely
  16|                       force the Town to become more proactive albeit with no identified source of funding. At the conclusion of
  17|                       winter and again in the late fall drainage structures in close proximity to open water are cleaned. Other
  18|                       structures throughout the Town are addressed as time and resources allow on an intermittent schedule.
  19|                       Waste Water
  20|                                    The DPW continues as the caretaker of the entire sewer system. In an effort to become more
  21|                       efficient the Sewer Commission has outsourced much of the day to day inspections and preventative
  22|                       maintenance of the overall wastewater system inclusive of 10 pump stations. Business management and
  23|                       oversight of the subcontractor remain the responsibility of the DPW.
  24|                       Tree Removal
  25|                                   While it may seem difficult to believe, the infamous "Ice Storm of '08" continues to detrimentally
  26|                       affect trees in the Town right-of-way. As presented to the Board of Selectman during the initial recovery
  27|                       process, the "heartwood" of a large volume of trees was affected. Previously unnoticed damage together
  28|                       with natural attrition of every species creates a backlog of tree felling and pruning that far exceeds the
  29|                       allotted budget. The department is unable to fulfill each resident request and must prioritize work based
  30|                       upon the calculated degree of danger to residents and property. A more efficient approach would involve
  31|                       a survey of all Town owned trees with a generated list of those requiring attention. Until a plan is in place,
  32|                       the DPW will act in a reactionary mode. All work aside from brush removal, chipping, and the felling of
  33|                       small diameter trees is outsourced due to the necessity of a bucket truck and a licensed professional. Each
  34|                       spring DPW staff initiates the activity of removing and disposing of woody debris within the right-of-way
  35|                       and a Town-wide program of curbside mowing.
  36|                       Landfill
  37|                                   The "capped" landfill off Young's Rd. remains in compliance with the inspection protocol
  38|                       mandated by the Division of Environmental Protection. The site is monitored regularly for excessive
  39|                       methane gas as well as the possibility of groundwater contamination.
  40|                                    The frequency of the testing was reduced through a special permit acquired as a result of
  41|                       consistently favorable results. The landfill site including the perimeter fencing is inspected on a regular
  42|                       schedule by DPW personnel.
  43|                                                                                                     57

===PAGE 58=== (ocr, 46 lines)
   1|                                    Adjacent to the "cap" is a storage area for catch basin materials and street sweepings both
   2|                        determined by the EPA to be hazardous waste. We are permitted to store these materials through the
   3|                       procurement of a (BUD) Beneficial Use Determination permit. The DEP requires yearly testing of these
   4|                       materials.
   5|                                    On weekends during the fall and springtime months DPW personnel oversee and manage the
   6|                       annual composting of brush, leaves and other organic debris providing a valuable service to our residents
   7|                       and add a valuable component to our recycling program. There has to date been no dedicated funding
   8|                       toward the organization or long range remediation of this location. Once again, dollars will be taken from
   9|                       the General Highway line to maintain this location while keeping it environmentally safe. Next year, a
  10|                       proposal to dispose of accumulated brush and trees will be submitted to the Capital Planning Committee
  11|                       for consideration in order to maintain the required space for resident disposal. The accumulation of leaves
  12|                       is formed into long manageable rows that are turned regularly and will over time revert to compost.
  13|                       Solid Waste
  14|                                    Public works monitors, orders, stores, and distributes trash bags in order to facilitate the curbside
  15|                       collection of trash and recyclables by our current vendor, Casella Inc.
  16|                       Lake Shirley Dam
  17|                       In the early 1990's, with the structure in need of repair/rebuilding The Lake Shirley Association turned
  18|                       over ownership of the dam to the Town. After completion of a total reconstruction, responsibilities for
  19|                       maintenance, monitoring, and record keeping was completed solely by a small number of volunteers from
  20|                       the Lake Association. In 2004-2005 custodianship of the dam, compliance with State dam regulations, the
  21|                        establishment of an operations manual as well as an emergency action plan was placed under the umbrella
  22|                       of the Department of Public Works. As with the storm water program and other EPA / DEP mandates
  23|                       compliance with current and future regulations is critical. We rely on the expertise and support of a
  24|                       professional consultant to assist with predetermined mandates. The most recent inspection resulted in a
  25|                       positive report.
  26|                       Winter Operations
  27|                                    Snow and ice present a major challenge to our Town. The safety of the general public depends on
  28|                       the ability of the DPW to maintain our roadways in a safe condition despite the severity or the duration of
  29|                       snow and ice events. To that end we develop a winter operations procedure based upon a detailed plan
  30|                       that must be flexible due to the unpredictability of each storm. A consistently high level of service is
  31|                       expected and must be delivered to every part of Town in a timely manner.
  32|                                    Departmental preparedness begins with successful implementation of the capital plan. Financial
  33|                       support is necessary to provide effective fleet rotation insuring minimal interruption of services due to
  34|                       breakdowns and repairs. Many of the front line vehicles are well beyond the optimum time for
  35|                       replacement. In the fall, salt and sand are delivered to the Chase Rd. facility. Lunenburg is in a
  36|                       consortium with 14 other communities in an effort to procure the lowest possible price for salt.
  37|                       Individually the Town also solicits bids for road sand. From late summer to early fall vehicle maintenance
  38|                       staff inspects and prepares the trucks, sanders and plows for winter operations. During the construction
  39|                       season road crews address right-of-way issues, overhanging branches, and pavement defects in order to
  40|                       eliminate obstacles to plowing. Each division within the DPW is involved in winter operations. Typically
  41|                       DPW staff combines with 18-20 subcontractors to provide service.
  42|                                    Generally it is not the amount of snow but the duration of the event that determines the overall
  43|                       cost. For example, a fast moving snow storm of 6-8 inches will cost significantly less than a long duration
  44|                       freezing rain event even though the accumulation is much less. Historically, the department operates in a
  45|                       deficit due to a yearly allocation that is below the cost of an average winter.
  46|                                                                                                     58

   1|                                                          SENIOR PROPERTY TAX WORK-OFF PROGRAM
   2|                                                                                              Est. 1998
   3|                                                    CALANDAR YEAR JANUARY 1, 2015 - NOVEMBER 1, 2015
   4|                        "A unique approach to balance the social & financial needs of senior homeowners and local governments
   5|                             of Massachusetts" Archhana Prakash, Post Doctoral Fellow of Population Studies at the Center of
   6|                                                                                     University of Michigan
   7|                       The Property Tax Work-Off Committee is a 5 member committee appointed by the Lunenburg Board of
   8|                       Selectmen.
   9|                       The Lunenburg Property Tax Work-Off Program offers income eligible senior citizens who are age 60
  10|                       plus an opportunity to receive up to $1,000 off their property tax bill in the calendar year rather than the
  11|                       fiscal year. Participants worked in various town departments to earn the tax abatement doing general
  12|                       office duties, custodial, library shelving, and kitchen assistance.
  13|                       For each hour worked a person received $10 and worked up to 100 hours between January 1, 2015 and
  14|                       November 1, 2015 to receive the abatement. Any hours worked beyond that were considered volunteer
  15|                       hours.
  16|                       There were nine Lunenburg residents who participated between January 1, 2015 and November 1, 2015.
  17|                       These individuals as a whole accumulated 865.5 hours towards their abatements.
  18|                       Eligibility Requirements:
  19|                             • Applicants must be 60 years of age or older
  20|                                   Own and occupy a home in Lunenburg as their primary residence for at least one year
  21|                             • Receive a property tax bill in their name or their spouse's name who is also 60 years of age or
  22|                                   older
  23|                             • Meet the income guidelines of :
  24|                                   One person household - $40,000 / Two person household - $60,000
  25|                             • All new applicants are required to have a CORI background check and must re- apply and be
  26|                                   accepted annually for participation in the program.
  27|                       Earnings are exempt from state taxes only. Earnings are subject to federal and FICA tax withholdings
  28|                       and are also subject to OBRA if participants are not receiving a pension from either Worcester Regional
  29|                       Retirement or Massachusetts State Teachers Retirement.
  30|                        Departments who participated between January 1, 2015 - November 1, 2015:
  31|                       Lunenburg Board of Health
  32|                       Lunenburg Building Department
  33|                        Lunenburg Council on Aging
  34|                       Lunenburg DP W/Sewer Departments
  35|                       Lunenburg Police Dept.
  36|                       Lunenburg Public Library

   1|                                                                                 SEWER COMMISSION
   2|                       The five member Sewer Commission was originally established at the Special Town Meeting on May 6, 2006.
   3|                       At the first Sewer Commission meeting after the May 2014 Town election, when the Commission elects the
   4|                        officers for the next year, Carl Luck was elected to remain as Chairman, Dave MacDonald to serve as Vice-
   5|                       Chair and Mike Nault to serve as Clerk. Other members on the Commission were Butch Bilotta and Troy
   6|                        Daniels, who was elected to the Sewer Commission in the May 2014 Town Election as a write-in candidate to
   7|                        fill the vacancy left by Jay Simeone who did not run for re-election. The Sewer Commission bears the
   8|                       responsibility of overseeing the Town's sewer system, planning for the future, and developing and implementing
   9|                       rules, regulations and policies. The Department of Public Works manages and maintains the operational side of
  10|                       the system. Under the Town's Charter, responsibility for the day-to day operation, care and maintenance of the
  11|                       sanitary sewers are under the supervision of the Town Manager. The Town of Lunenburg does not operate a
  12|                       sewer treatment plant. Approximately 81% of Lunenburg sewer is discharged to the City of Leominster, and the
  13|                       other 19% is discharged to the City of Fitchburg.
  14|                        There are currently 764 properties connected to the Lunenburg system and another 378 that have access to Town
  15|                        Sewer but are not yet connected. During FY15, 36 new accounts connected to Town Sewer. The Commission
  16|                       billed out $715,400 in quarterly sewer bills, and had $41,759 of prior year delinquencies added to the owners'
  17|                       property tax bills for non-payment. Nine properties with access to sewer were assessed privilege fees that had
  18|                       not originally been assessed betterments. Privilege fees help to pay down the debt owed by the Town on the
  19|                       original sewer project.
  20|                       In FY15, it was required by the State Department of Revenue that the Sewer Enterprise and the Sewer
  21|                       Betterment Funds be combined for a consolidated statement, and for the first time, the Commission had to
  22|                       project the year-to-year income over expense as pertains to betterment income versus debt service. With these
  23|                       revisions to the budget, it was necessary to request a transfer from Retained Earnings for $77,401.80 (Article 17,
  24|                        May 2015 Town Meeting) to cover both general expenses and debt service for the next fiscal year. The goal of
  25|                       the Sewer Commission is to maintain a balanced budget going forward and to build up the Retained Earnings so
  26|                       that it may be used for major capital projects to maintain and improve the operating efficiency of the system.
  27|                       In August 2013, the Sewer Commission began contracting with Small Water Systems Services of Littleton
  28|                       (SWSS) for the Operations and Management of the 10 pumping stations and sewer infrastructure. The Sewer
  29|                       Commission has been very satisfied with the personnel, the work and the arrangement with SWSS, renewing the
  30|                       contract again for FY15. Since the start of the contract, additional responsibilities have been added to the SWSS
  31|                       contract, including installing and monitoring the SCADA system at the Leominster Road station in March 2015
  32|                       and taking on the maintenance of the 10 generators housed in our pumping stations.
  33|                       The Sewer Commission continued work on preparing for the major sewer project in the Pratt Street/Lakeview
  34|                       Ave sections of town, using the State Revolving Fund (SRF) program throughout FY15, to connect 80 plus
  35|                       homes in areas of need as determined by the Comprehensive Wastewater Management Plan to public sewer.
  36|                        Forty-two of these homes were in close proximity to Whalom Lake and were of concern to the homeowners,
  37|                        Board of Health and environmentalists. The proposed sewer extensions had attained a satisfactory rating by the
  38|                       State to be assured of an SRF loan and the Commission presented the project at the spring Town Meeting in
  39|                       May 2014, obtaining approval to move the project forward. The Commission worked continuously with the
  40|                       engineering firm, Wright Pierce, throughout the year on design and engineering. In the spring of 2015, the
  41|                       Commission put the project out to bid and in May 2015 awarded the construction bid to CJP Construction out of
  42|                        Millis, MA, with construction to commence in the summer of 2015.
  43|                       Also in the spring of 2015, the Commission, working with Weston & Sampson Engineering, continued their
  44|                       work to find sources of I/I (Inflow/Infiltration) by performing 171 house-to-house inspections in the Mass
  45|                       Ave./Leominster Rd. areas in the spring of 2015. These efforts were funded by the Sewer Bank Fee, established
  46|                       in 2013 as required by the Inter-Municipal Agreement with the City of Leominster, collecting $220. per
  47|                       bedroom on new connections. Weston & Sampson worked to ensure proper connections from these 171
  48|                                                                                                     70

===PAGE 71=== (ocr, 39 lines)
   1|                       locations to the public sewer and advising those property owners when an illegal connection was discovered,
   2|                       whether it is from a sump pump in the cellar or roof drain. These sources only increase the town's expenses as
   3|                       they are sent via public sewer pipes to the wastewater treatment plants in either Leominster or Fitchburg,
   4|                       increasing their flows and capacities unnecessarily.
   5|                       The Commission has continued to work hard to enforce the Grease Trap Regulation for all Food Service
   6|                       Establishments that have or should have a grease trap or grease interceptor. Annual permit fees were assessed
   7|                       in July 2015 based on the establishment's level of compliance, and the reporting requirements clearly
   8|                       communicated. Lunenburg has 19 grease trap establishments. This regulation will continue to be strongly
   9|                       enforced as fats, oils and grease (FOG) can negatively affect the smooth operation and maintenance costs of the
  10|                       sewer system. While the Grease Trap Regulation focuses on commercial and public disposal, individual home
  11|                       owners can also contribute a significant amount of grease into the system which increases everyone's costs. The
  12|                       Commission understands that education is an important aspect of their role and will continue to provide
  13|                       information to their customers to keep the sewer system running economically and efficiently by reducing the
  14|                       disposal of fats, oil and grease into the system to avoid blockages. Whether on sewer or septic, grease should not
  15|                       be put down the drain. Another enemy of the sewer system is "disposable wipes" which do not biodegrade and
  16|                       bring our pumps to a halt. Nothing but organic waste and toilet paper should be put into the sewer system.
  17|                       During FY15 and into FY16, the Commission continued working on several projects, with Commissioners
  18|                       serving as Project Champions. They are:
  19|                             • Lakeview/Pratt extension
  20|                             • I/I reduction project
  21|                             • Grease trap compliance
  22|                             • Flow Rate/Metering
  23|                             • Privately Funded Extension Policy update
  24|                            • Business Systems and Process Improvement
  25|                       The Commission would like to thank Dave Mac Donald and Butch Bilotta, who both stepped off the
  26|                       Commission in May 2015, for all their hard work and years of dedication and service. In the town election of
  27|                       May 2015, the Commission was happy to welcome Sue Bunish to the Commission, and John Reynolds who was
  28|                       appointed to the Commission in July 2015. Troy Daniels stepped off the Commission in January 2016. Bob
  29|                       Ebersole continues to serve as the Board of Selectmen liaison and the Commission is grateful for his knowledge
  30|                       and counsel. Jay Simeone, past member of the Sewer Commission, serves as the Finance Committee liaison to
  31|                       blend his experience on the Commission with its financial planning and we thank him for his participation. The
  32|                       Commission would also like to thank Jack Rodriquenz, DPW Director, for the seamless and smooth operation of
  33|                       the Sewer division of the DPW and also Jim Breault (DPW-Facilities) who whenever called upon, provides his
  34|                       expertise and service to the Sewer Department.

   1|                                                                                 BOARD OF HEALTH
   2|                        The Board of Health office is located in the Ritter Library Building on the corner of Mass. Ave and
   3|                        Leominster Road. Our office is on the upper level at the end of the hall on the right. We can be reached at
   4|                        978-345-4146, extension 430.
   5|                        The Board of Health with the assistance of its agent, the Nashoba Associated Boards of Health, continued
   6|                       its mission to maintain its focus on public health and safety issues during 2015, by reviewing Title V
   7|                        inspection reports, building permits, septic and well permits, nuisance investigations, housing inspections,
   8|                        complaints and general public health related issues.
   9|                        This past year has seen the reinstatement of the Septic System Repair Program which helps low to
  10|                        moderate income families replace failed septic systems or connect to public sewer. Anyone interested in
  11|                        finding out more about this program can contact the Board of Health office.
  12|                        Homeland Security planning is ongoing. Meetings continue between our agents, other Town Departments
  13|                        and regional entities to develop a plan for not only Lunenburg but also with our partner towns in our
  14|                        region.
  15|                        This year we processed applications for septic permit lot tests, permits for new construction, new wells,
  16|                        repairs or upgrades to septic systems and well permits. The Board continues its vigilance with regard to
  17|                        septic systems, wells, food service inspections, housing and nuisance complaints and its general mandate to
  18|                        protect the environment and groundwaters of the Commonwealth. The Board of Health is also represented
  19|                        on the recently created Stormwater Task Force.
  20|                        The Board of Health provides numerous other services in cooperation with our health agents, the Nashoba
  21|                        Associated Boards of Health. In addition to our environmental services, numerous clinics are provided
  22|                        throughout the year to our residents. These clinics provide inoculations, blood pressure screenings, Well
  23|                        Oldster Clinics and dental screening. Fluoride treatment and dental checks of our youngsters in the school
  24|                        system are provided by the Nashoba dental staff.
  25|                        The Town of Lunenburg participates in the Central Mass. Mosquito Control Project. Mosquito Control
  26|                        monitors the mosquito population in Lunenburg and advises of any potential diseases such as EEE and
  27|                        West Nile Virus. It sprays frequently to control the population during the warmer times of the year.
  28|                        Residents who want to have their property sprayed can do so by emailing to: cmmcp@cmmcp.org, calling
  29|                       (508) 393-3055, completing a service request on their webpage at: http://www.cmmcp.org or calling the
  30|                        Board of Health office.
  31|                        Along with our Nashoba Nursing and Hospice partners, we provide in-home visits to residents recovering
  32|                        from illness and hospice care and counseling to those in need of this service.
  33|                        Please remember that our Board members volunteer their time and efforts on behalf of you, the citizens of
  34|                        Lunenburg. If you have something that you think we can help you with, we are at your service. Contact the
  35|                        Board of Health office at 582-4146 ext. 430.

   2|                                                                                   655 Massachusetts Ave

   7|                                                                                          118
   8|                           The Firefighters and Emergency Medical Technicians of the Lunenburg Fire Department are dedicated to
   9|                           providing the highest quality, most cost effective fire and emergency medical services to the citizens of the
  10|                                                                                        Town of Lunenburg.
  11|                                       In 2015 your Fire Department responded to 1985 calls for service, broken down as follows:
  12|                                                 Fires & Hazardous Conditions                   483                  Emergency Medical                967
  13|                                                    Inspections      493                                                Other                        37
  14|                           Fire Department staffing today is five Career Staff and forty to forty-five On Call Firefighters and Emergency
  15|                       Medical Technicians. The station is staffed 7 days per week from 6:00 a.m. - 6:00 p.m. The career staff man the
  16|                       station Monday through Friday. On Saturday and Sunday the station is manned by two of our On Call
  17|                       Firefighter/EMTs on an hourly "per diem" basis. At night however, all of our personnel respond from home on
  18|                       an "on call" basis. This adds several minutes or more to our response time as personnel must respond to the
  19|                       station, pick up the appropriate equipment and then respond the call.
  20|                            The addition of the Weekend Day coverage began on July 1, 2015 and has significantly decreased response
  21|                       times during the time the station is manned. This is the first significant change to our staffing in nearly 15 years,
  22|                       even though we have seen an almost 48% increase in our call volume during that same time period. We still rely
  23|                       on our On Call Personnel to be the primary responders 50% of the week.
  24|                           2015 was our busiest year to date, with a 1.5% overall increase in activity from 2014 and a 5.5% increase in
  25|                       EMS related calls. As our community continues to grow I can only expect the demand for emergency services to
  26|                       grow along with it. While our Call Force continues to do an amazing job, the ever increasing call volume is
  27|                       straining our ability to provide the high level of service townspeople have come to expect. This leads me to
  28|                       continue to call for 24 hour staffing in the station. Funding to maintain 2 Firefighter/EMT's in the station 24
  29|                       hours a day, 7 days a week would allow either the first ambulance or first piece of fire apparatus to respond
  30|                       immediately. Not only would this reduce our response times to critical emergencies, it would also reduce the
  31|                       "wear and tear" on our Call Staff. This coverage would in no way reduce the need for our On Call personnel; it
  32|                       would only supplement their response and reduce response times.
  33|                             Our firefighters continue to train for the myriad of situations which can be encountered even in a town such as
  34|                       ours. Today's firefighter must be skilled in not only firefighting, but medical care, hazardous materials mitigation
  35|                       and technical rescue. Our EMT's must continue to stay abreast of the latest treatment protocols and advances in
  36|                       lifesaving skills. Personnel train regularly both here at the station and at classes sponsored by other agencies.
  37|                        While they are compensated for some of the training, the vast majority is done on their own time.
  38|                                                                                                     81

===PAGE 82=== (ocr, 46 lines)
   1|                                   As an example, a new Firefighter/EMT must attend over 340 hours of basic firefighting and Emergency
   2|                       Medical Technician training. Once they are certified, they must complete over 40 hours of continuing education
   3|                       and refresher training every two years, just for their EMT. Operators of Fire Apparatus must complete an
   4|                       additional 65 hours of training in Driver training, pump and aerial operation and hydraulics calculations.
   5|                                   Several of our personnel are members of Regional Technical Rescue units, providing services for
   6|                       Confined Space and Cave in Rescue, as well as Underwater Search and Recovery. They stand ready to respond as
   7|                       needed throughout Northern Worcester County.
   8|                                   2015 continued to be an active year for our Fire Prevention efforts. By law we are required to inspect
   9|                       smoke and carbon monoxide detector installations when a home is sold, as well as all new oil burner and propane
  10|                       gas installations. Any business holding a liquor license is also required to be inspected for fire safety issues. In
  11|                       addition, all new construction projects must have their plans reviewed for proper fire protection, as well as
  12|                       ongoing inspections during the construction process. Personnel also continue to provide fire safety education to
  13|                                   Other Fire Safety Initiatives undertaken during 2015 include:
  14|                                   - Continuation of a Department of Fire Services Grant in the amount of $6953. to assist with Fire
  15|                                        Safety Education in both the schools and with senior citizens. This grant provides funding for both
  16|                                        materials and personnel to bring fire safety education to our most vulnerable populations. Highlights
  17|                                        of activity through this grant include:
  18|                                                 Educational programs in basic fire safety in Grades K-3, including use of the Regional Fire
  19|                                                    Safety Trailer.
  20|                                              • Educational programs in conjunction with the Council on Aging. These included cooking
  21|                                                    and heating safety, a CPR Demonstration and ice safety.
  22|                                        Participation in the Senior Center's "Sand for Seniors" Program. This program provides buckets of
  23|                                        walkway sand for senior citizens who were unable to obtain it for themselves in the winter months.
  24|                                        In partnership with this program, our Fire Prevention Officer Captain James Ricci delivers the sand to
  25|                                        the residents and when possible, inspects their homes for smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. If
  26|                                        the resident was lacking detectors, Capt. Ricci would install free detectors obtained through the
  27|                                        Senior SAFE Grant.
  28|                                       The Department also partnered with the American Red Cross to install free smoke detectors in
  29|                                        sections of town. Combined with the "Sand of Seniors" program, 93 homes were visited and over 70 smoke and carbon monoxide detectors were installed.
  30|                                        It should be noted that each year, 50% of fatal fires are found to have nonfunctional or nonexistent
  31|                                        smoke detectors.
  32|                                   Several members are also Certified First Aid and CPR Instructors and provide training to both citizens
  33|                       and town employees.
  34|                                   Our department continues to actively pursue grant funding opportunities as they occur, though those
  35|                       opportunities are becoming scarcer.
  36|                                   The new Engine 1, approved in the FY '15 Capital Plan was placed in service in July of 2015 and is
  37|                       providing outstanding service as our primary pumper. It replaced a 1991 model.
  38|                       Apparatus replacement continues to be a concern. FY'15 saw a significant increase in vehicle maintenance costs,
  39|                       particularly with the older apparatus. The timely replacement of our older apparatus will hopefully decrease some
  40|                       of those costs. Two of our front line units (Engine 4 and Ladder 1) are over 20 years old and showing their age
  41|                       through increasing maintenance costs and "out of service" time. Engine 4 in particular has seen over $50,000 in
  42|                       repairs over the last 3 years, and has averaged a month per year out of service. The new Engine 1 is handing a
  43|                       higher volume of responses to decrease the wear and tear on Engine 4, hopefully prolonging its lifespan. These
  44|                       units are included the department's 5 Year Capital Plan for replacement in FY '17 and FY '18 respectively and it
  45|                       is hoped that due consideration will be given for their timely replacement.
  46|                                                                                                     82

   2|                       difficult to maintain as these units reach the end of their life span.

   5|                       provides the basic skills firefighters need to operate in today's challenging environments. All newly hired

  10|                       are Emergency Medical Technicians to obtain real world experience as firefighters while completing their
  11|                       education. It also provides the department with additional assistance as these members cover some On Call shifts
  12|                       from the station.
