  13|                                                                              State of the Police Department
  14|                        The Police Department is in operation 24 hours a day 7 days a week. Two patrol officers are assigned to
  15|                       each shift with support from the Traffic Enforcement/K-9 Officer and the Community Outreach Officer
  16|                       who each work two day shifts and two evening shifts. A Reserve Officer is assigned to the desk on a full
  17|                       time basis from 7:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. Monday through Friday. The desk is extended from 3:00 p.m. to
  18|                       7:00 p.m. during the week on a per-diem basis.
  19|                       The Police were dispatched to approximately 5600 calls for service and self-initiated another 7800 calls,
  20|                       responded to 278 motor vehicle accidents, investigated 1253 incidents, conducted 4039 motor vehicle
  21|                       stops, wrote 2440 motor vehicle citations, arrested 371 people, summonsed 259, and placed 12 people in
  22|                       protective custody.
  23|                       In addition to the calls dispatched by the regional call center, the desk officer answered some 7000 phone
  24|                       calls, took approximately 3200 lobby inquiries and complaints, and wrote, roughly, 153 reports in 2015.
  25|                       This year the desk watch officer was responsible for the suicide watch of 146 detainees either taken into
  26|                       custody overnight or during the daytime hours.
  27|                       In the past five years the police department has realized a 180.1 percent increase in arrests, a 61.9%
  28|                       increase in reportable incidents, incidents that require a follow-up investigation and/ or court complaint,
  29|                       and a 20% increase in motor vehicle accidents. I don't anticipate that these figures are going to decline as
  30|                       the Town continues to grow and the level of traffic in and around Lunenburg increases.

   1|                                                                    CAPITAL PLANNING COMMITTEE
   2|                        Lunenburg's Charter specifically mandates that a Capital Planning Committee prepare a Fiscal Year (FY)
   3|                        Plan and a Capital Improvement Plan. These Plans are to be presented to the Town Manager.
   4|                        As noted in the past reports, the criterion for any capital request includes Mandates, Safety, Need, Crisis,
   5|                        Cost Effectiveness and Ability to Fund. The Committee has to review each request under these six
   6|                        elements. Not only do they have to determine that the request fits within the criteria, but they have to
   7|                       prioritize the level that meets the criteria. Therefore, not all requests are included in the FY Plans, mostly
   8|                        due to funding. The result of the proposed FY Plans provides the needed service for safety and protection
   9|                       of the public, the upkeep to our schools and the management of government.
  10|                        At the Annual Town Meeting May 2015, the following items, totaling $ 1,051,578, were presented in the

   1|                                                                                ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS
   2|                       The Zoning Board of Appeals conducted fourteen hearings during calendar year 2015, all for special permits. Thirteen of the
   3|                       requested special permits were granted and one was denied. There were no applications for variances.
   4|                       The Zoning Board meets on the second and fourth Wednesdays of the month on an "as needed" basis. The members are:
   5|                       Raymond E. Beal, Chairman, Donald F. Bowen, Vice Chairman, James Besarkarski, Alfred Gravelle, Hans Wentrup and
   6|                       associate members, David Blatt, Paul Doherty and Sheila Lumi. Lisa Normandin is the Administrative Assistant to the
   7|                       Zoning Board.
   8|                       The functions of the Zoning Board of Appeals as required by statutes are as follows:
   9|                                   To hear and decide applications for Variances from the Town's Protective Bylaws as authorized in
  10|                                   the Bylaws.
  11|                             2. To hear and decide applications for Special Permits as authorized in the Town's Protective Bylaws.
  12|                             3. To hear and decide appeals in accordance with Chapter 40A, Section 8 of the Massachusetts
  13|                                   General Laws, as amended, from any person aggrieved by reason of his or her inability to obtain
  14|                                   a permit or enforcement action from the Administrative Officer or Board in the Town, the
  15|                                   Regional Planning Agency, abutting City or Town or other Administrative Official.
  16|                             4. To act upon application for comprehensive permits in accordance with Massachusetts General
  17|                                   Laws, Chapter 40B. The Zoning Board of Appeals reviews requests for comprehensive permits
  18|                                   submitted to the Board under Chapter 40B by developers who wish to create affordable housing.
  19|                                   These requests can by law, circumvent local zoning ordinances.
  20|                       The Office of the Zoning Board of Appeals is located in the Ritter Memorial Building, 960 Massachusetts
  21|                       Avenue. If you need any assistance from the Zoning Board of Appeals, please contact Lisa Normandin at 978-582-4146 X
  22|                       421 during regular business hours. Zoning Board applications (with instructions) are available from the office.

   1|                          The building project has its own website at our district website www.lunenburgschools.net and Facebook page -
   2|                         Lunenburg Middle/High School Building Project. The District will return to a four school configuration with the
   3|                         opening of the new co-located middle/high school in August, 2016. Each building will have a smaller student
   4|                         population than the current configuration. The Primary School will serve students PK-2. Grades 3-5 will be at
   5|                         Turkey Hill Elementary School. Grades 6-12 will be in the new co-located middle/high school.
   6|                         The new school was designed to operate as two separate educational programs. The new building has a classroom
   7|                         wing for the middle school and another classroom wing for high school. The 6th grade students will be located
   8|                          on the first floor of the middle school wing. Classrooms for grades 7 and 8 are located on the second floor of the
   9|                         middle school wing. Middle school and high school students will enter the building via separate entrances.
  10|                         Located behind the classroom wings are the cafeteria, gym, auditorium, central offices, health services, and
  11|                         library/media center. There are an appropriate number of art, music, and technology classrooms for both middle
  12|                         and high school programs which are clustered together in the central core of the building near the auditorium. On
  13|                         the second floor above the school offices there are foreign language classrooms. The gymnasium can be divided at
  14|                         center court by a curtain to accommodate two large physical education classes. There is also a weight room and
  15|                         an alternate physical education room with a substantial dance/yoga area, exercise bikes and treadmills. There are
  16|                         two locker rooms for the middle school students and two locker rooms for the high school students. A health
  17|                         education classroom is also located near the gym.
  18|                         Lauren Drury Basque is the 2015 Superintendent's Award recipient. She is the daughter of Kenneth and Suzanne
  19|                          Basque. At LHS Lauren focused her studies on the sciences including numerous honors and advanced placement
  20|                                       She is ranked first in her class. Lauren was honored at the Worcester County Superintendent's
  21|                         Roundtable Scholars' ceremony in January. She selected a quote from Eleanor Roosevelt for that ceremony's
  22|                         program. The quote certainly captures the essence of this remarkable young woman. "The purpose of life is to
  23|                         live it, to taste experience to the utmost, to reach out eagerly and without fear for newer and richer experience."
  24|                         Ms. Basque personifies our mission for lifelong learning and responsible community membership; constantly
  25|                         learning, growing, achieving and giving. She inspires us with her joy of learning and service to her community.

  24|                                                                                          School Facilities
  25|                                                                                              2015-2016
  26|                       Construction of the new Middle School/High School continued throughout the year with completion of the
  27|                       building expected by late May 2016. Shawmut Construction Management continues to execute the building
  28|                       project with NV5, having acquired Joslin, Lesser, & Associates, providing owner's project management services.
  29|                       The School Building Committee continues to provide construction and financial oversight. The exterior envelope
  30|                       was completed by the fall of 2015 which allowed for interior finish work to continue throughout the following
  31|                       winter. The project continued on time and budget despite the challenges of substantial snowfall in February 2015.
  32|                       Phase 2, which includes construction of the new greenhouse, removal of asbestos in the high school as well as
  33|                       demolition, construction of two athletic fields, modifying the student parking lot, tennis courts, construction of an
  34|                       outdoor basketball court and remaining site work will commence in June 2016. Phase 2 is expected to be 2225
  35|                       complete by late December 2016.
  36|                       The FY 16 capital plan approved funding of the district technology plan at $36,200. The FY 15 capital plan
  37|                       funded $138,000 for asbestos abatement at Turkey Hill Middle School which had been unable to be completed
  38|                       during the summer of 2014. In July 2015, four classrooms had abatement work (removal of tile ceilings,
  39|                       abatement of spray-on fireproofing and vinyl asbestos tiles) completed and returned to a usable condition for the
  40|                       school year at a cost of $119,803. Montachusett Contracting Company Inc. completed the work by August 1,
  41|                       2015. Unexpended funds are expected to be utilized to continue asbestos abatement at Turkey Hill Middle School.
  42|                       The focus of school maintenance for FY16 continues to be preventative maintenance of heating,
  43|                       ventilation systems and energy conservation measures particularly of the schools that will operate in FY
  44|                       17. Conversion of existing lighting to LED remains a high priority for Lunenburg Primary School and
  45|                       Turkey Hill Middle School. Preparations for the reorganization of the district in June 2016 were also a
  46|                       focus area throughout the year. Identifying materials that need to move as part of the reorganization and
  47|                       determining the disposition of furniture and equipment that will be surplus once the new school building
  48|                       opens has been ongoing since July 2015. This                                 102

===PAGE 103=== (ocr, 44 lines)
   1|                       will culminate with a contractor move of teaching supplies to the new building in June 2016 and the removal of
   2|                       all non-fixed items from the current high school by the end of June 2016.
   3|                       During the year, we have continued to fine tune plans for two LED conversion projects using Green Community
   4|                       Funds. The project for Turkey Hill Middle School is to convert all 28 Watt florescent lamps to 18 Watt LED
   5|                       lamps at a cost of $36,253 with a resultant 6.7 year payback in energy savings. At Lunenburg Primary School,
   6|                       conversion of high bay fixtures in the gym and media center to LED are also planned as well as conversion of 28
   7|                       Watt fluorescent lamps at a cost of $44,145 with a 6.4 year pay back.
   8|                       For the FY 17 Capital Program, the School Department has requested an additional $145,000 in funding for
   9|                       continued asbestos removal at Turkey Hill as its highest priority. Two unfunded
  10|                       FY 16 requests to replace the Turkey Hill phone system and intercom system at $22,000 each were priorities 2

  42|                                   The Lunenburg Primary School is devoted to providing quality early childhood education for students
  43|                       Preschool to 3"d grade. Our students range from three years old to nine years old. Our community is made up of
  44|                       students, parents, teachers and support staff, working together to create an educationally rich and safe learning
  45|                       environment for our children.
  46|                       The October 1, 2015 student count reported to the department of Elementary and Secondary Education was five
  47|                       hundred and three students. Our Preschool program services thirty-eight three and four year old
  48|                                                                                                    105

   1|                                   students. We have five Kindergarten classes servicing ninety-nine students. Class sizes in our
   2|                       Kindergartens are 20 students. First grade has one hundred and fifteen students with class sizes ranging from 22 -
   3|                        23. Second grade has one hundred and thirty-three students with class sizes ranging from 26-27 students and the
   4|                        third grade has one hundred and twenty-two students with class sizes ranging from 24-25. We are utilizing all
   5|                       available space in the building to provide a child-centered educational program for all our students.
   6|                                   We constantly strive to find better ways to meet the collective as well as the individual needs of our
   7|                       students. Our Professional Development focused on Teacher Evaluation, Reading, Behavioral Intervention
   8|                        strategies and our new Everyday Math program materials. All of our classroom teachers continued to use
   9|                       Responsive Classroom strategies as part of our Academic/Social/Emotional Learning Curriculum which includes
  10|                       morning meetings, guided discovery, rules and logical consequences and academic choice. Teachers this past
  11|                        year completed curriculum maps and served on committees to revise and improve our ELA Curriculum and our
  12|                       Social Studies Curriculum.
  13|                                   The Primary School is a Title One school and we have continued our tiered instructional system to insure
  14|                        that all students have the services they need to be successful. Common assessments are completed in the fall,
  15|                        winter, and spring for all children in grades K-3 in the areas of reading, writing, and math.                                        These common
  16|                        assessments serve to monitor the effectiveness of teacher instruction and drive individual student instruction.
  17|                       Struggling students are identified quickly and additional resources and instruction are provided to address the
  18|                       areas of concern identified. Tiered instructional services are provided in the area of Language Arts and Math.
  19|                       The tiered instructional model requires that the teachers not only meet the needs of the students who may be
  20|                       struggling with learning but those students who are doing well and need to achieve higher levels of learning.
  21|                       Learning is becoming more personalized and students are being challenged to be confident, independent learners
  22|                        and problem solvers.
  23|                                   Our third graders participated in the Spring 2015 MCAS Assessment in the areas of ELA and Math. We
  24|                       work to make sure that students feel confident and prepared to take this assessment for the first time. All teachers
  25|                       have worked over the last several years to prepare them to be independent confident learners.

   1|                                                                            LUNENBURG HIGH SCHOOL
   2|                                                                                              2015-2016
   3|                       Lunenburg High School has been a hub for academic and social activity in 2015-2016. We have begun
   4|                       transitioning from our current building to the new Lunenburg Middle High School. The transition process is far
   5|                       bigger than just moving from one building to another. With the middle and high school in the same building,
   6|                       there are some challenges, but many opportunities to enhance the educational experiences of our students. A lot
   7|                       of planning and decisions have been made to ensure that we will be moving into a state-of-the-art school which
   8|                       will support 21" century learning. The building process has gone very smoothly and our students and educators
   9|                       are already looking forward to the start of school in August.
  10|                        As time has gone on, there is much more of a comfort level and stability in our grade 8-12 community. This
  11|                       year, we oriented 116 eighth grade students, four teachers, and six staff members to our building and school
  12|                       culture. With the assistance of 40 student leaders, we successfully transitioned the eighth grade students into the
  13|                       LHS culture by having an eighth grade orientation on the first day of school. We opened the year, as we do every
  14|                       year, with the District Attorney and Assistant District Attorney from Worcester County to discuss responsible
  15|                       Internet use, Facebook, cyber-bullying, Internet safety, drug use, and the power of making good choices with our
  16|                       incoming students and parents.
  17|                       NEASC ACCREDITATION
  18|                       Lunenburg High School completed a Five Year Report for the Commission on Public Secondary Schools of the
  19|                       New England Association of Schools and Colleges. In 2010, the Commission recommended that the school
  20|                       receive continued accreditation in the Association. The Commission's decision was based upon review of an
  21|                       evaluation report prepared by a visiting committee in April 2010. The Two Year Progress Report, submitted in
  22|                       January, 2013 received high marks from the Commission reviewing our submission. The Mid-Cycle Progress
  23|                       Report was reviewed and accepted by the Commission. One more Special Progress Report needs to be filed with
  24|                       the Commission in September. It will certify that the building project is complete and LHS will be taken off of
  25|                       "Warning" status and given full accreditation.
  26|                       SCHOOL/COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIPS
  27|                        Throughout the year, Lunenburg High School students are involved in a multitude of fundraising and collection
  28|                       endeavors. In the fall, three staff members were involved in a fundraiser to raise money for the Lunenburg Food
  29|                       Pantry. Money was collected during lunch and the staff member who raised the most money, got a pie in the face
  30|                       from a student at the Thanksgiving Academic Achievement Rally. Fun was had by all, and all of the proceeds
  31|                        were donated for the holiday season.
  32|                       Lunenburg High School received a generous donation in the amount of $500 from Mr. Mike's Mobil in
  33|                       Lunenburg, MA. The grant is to be used toward STEM initiatives at the high school. We are in the process of
  34|                       purchasing a new robot for our Robotics class.
  35|                       Hannaford Helps Schools made a donation of $1,000 last spring, which was earmarked for student activities. In
  36|                       addition, Hannaford donated an additional $500 from their receipt sales, which will benefit other activities at
  37|                       LHS.
  38|                       In March, the National Honor Society will be having its annual Blood Drive. Students sixteen and over (and staff
  39|                       members) will be able to participate in the Blood Drive with parent permission.
  40|                       The Media 2.0 Club has launched the Knightly News, which is an online newspaper. Students report on school
  41|                       activities, post film reviews, write political commentaries, and upload pictures of things going on inside and
  42|                       outside of LHS.
  43|                        LHS has held evening presentations for parents/guardians on the following topics:
  44|                             • Planning for High School (grade 8)

  10|                         (and society face) with distracted driving. There was a big emphasis on the dangers of texting while driving. The
  11|                         presentation was made possible by a donation from North End Subaru. A crashed car was located in the back
  12|                         parking lot of the school. The car was placed at the school by Quality Towing and Recovery. SADD provided
  13|                         the students with information about distracted driving during the course of the week and had students and staff
  14|                         pledge to not text and drive. During an Advisory period, SADD showed the short video, The Last Text.
  15|                          We have started an Advisory program at LHs. Une goal of Advisory is to have students have at least one adult
  16|                         who will get to know him/her over the course of four years. Students were randomly distributed into small grade-
  17|                         level groups who they will stay with during the four year period. Another goal of Advisory is to develop
  18|                         relationships with students of different backgrounds and social groups so that students can get to know each other
  19|                         and develop an appreciation of the diversity that we do have in Lunenburg.

   1|                        The 2014-2015 school year was my first year as Superintendent-Director of Montachusett Regional
   2|                        Vocational Technical School District, and it seemed to come and go in a minute; I would be remiss if I did
   3|                        not take time to reflect upon the numerous achievements our talented students, faculty and staff
   4|                       accomplished throughout the school year. These awards, recognitions, and distinctions are the result of years
   5|                       of high quality education and vocational-technical training. They are the hallmark of a Monty Tech
   6|                       education, earned by both individuals' and team efforts. While they are, in deed, an honor, they are simply a
   7|                       snapshot of the wonderful experiences happening on a day-to-day basis here at Monty Tech. I am delighted
   8|                       to present the District's 2014-2015 annual report to you, highlighting some of the year's most notable
   9|                       achievements, including:
  10|                        • A talented team of three Monty Tech Engineering students won the gold medal for Engineering
  11|                              Technology and Design at the SkillsUSA national competitions held in Louisville, KY. Nicolas Wicker
  12|                             of Fitchburg, Leon Gaulin of Winchendon and Devan Kumar, also of Winchendon, led by instructor
  13|                              Dennis Cormier, created a portable game console designed with retro gaming in mind. The team has
  14|                              developed patents on their prize-winning efforts, and continues to expand their business and engineering
  15|                              acumen.
  16|                       • The Machine Technology program aligned curriculum to MASSMEP (Massachusetts Manufacturing
  17|                              Extension Partnership) standards, and as a result students are now able to earn Level 1 and Level 2
  18|                              Applied Manufacturing Technology Pathway Certifications. Having these certifications will ensure
  19|                             program graduates stand-out when they enter the workforce upon graduation, as employers are better
  20|                             able to verify technical skills and expertise with this widely accepted training model. Also, our
  21|                              instructors are now able to access the manufacturing curriculum developed through Worcester
  22|                              Polytechnic Institute, adding rigor and relevance to our very popular Machine Technology program.
  23|                       • The Monty Tech Auto Body/ Collision Repair Department was featured in the April 2015 edition of the
  24|                              of the Alliance of Automotive Service Providers, Massachusetts cited the program's innovative
  25|                             technologies, spacious facilities, and specialized equipment as among the best in New England.
  26|                       • Outpacing more than 1,000 teams across the United States, and competing in three categories: network
  27|                             security, digital forensics, and Cisco networking, a team of six talented students captured first place at
  28|                             the CyberPatriot event, a national high school cyber defense competition, founded by the Air Force
  29|                              Association.
  30|                       • Students at Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School continued to demonstrate high
  31|                             academic achievement. In the spring of 2015, Monty Tech's passing rate on the MCAS English
  32|                              Language Arts exam was 100%, Mathematics 98%, and Biology 98%.
  33|                        We are so proud of the educational programs offered here at Monty Tech, yet we continually strive to
  34|                       improve upon them. Collaborating with area colleges and universities, we are ensuring our curriculum and
  35|                       instruction are rigorous and relevant. Sharing best practices with vocational-technical colleagues from across
  36|                       the state - and nation - we give and take some of the best ideas, with one thing in mind - what is best for our
  37|                       students. And what is best, I believe, is preparing students for both college and career.
  38|                       We hope you will find this report a comprehensive review of the quality education you have come to know
  39|                       and expect from Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School. You may notice that each of the
  40|                        eighteen member cities and towns are reflected in this report, and that students performed services in almost
  41|                       every community last year. Providing our students with an opportunity to give back to the communities that
  42|                       support them - and support our school - is a pleasure.
  43|                                                                                                                      Respectfully submitted,
  44|                                                                                                                      Sheila M. Harrity, Ed.D. heila M. Darity
  45|                                                                                                                      Superintendent-Director

   2|                       Every student will graduate from Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School with the skills,
   3|                       knowledge, and abilities to be a productive and effective member of an ever-changing society.
   4|                                                                                            Our District
   5|                       Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School is a four-year career and technical high school serving
   6|                       the member towns of:

  13|                                                                                             Leadership
  14|                       The leadership team at Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School is comprised of ten talented
  15|                       administrators whose varied educational backgrounds, professional experiences, and areas of expertise
  16|                       contribute to the success of the school. Working collaboratively, and under the direction of the
  17|                       Superintendent and Principal, the team has been able to transform the school into one of the most sought-
  18|                       after high schools in North Central Massachusetts.

  24|                                                                                             Enrollment
  25|                       On June 1, 2015, student enrollment at Monty Tech included 1,418 students in grades nine through twelve.
  26|                       Students are represented from every community in the district: Ashburnham (61), Ashby (35), Athol (88),
  27|                       Barre (37), Fitchburg (368), Gardner (146), Harvard (5), Holden (71), Hubbardston (62), Lunenburg (78),
  28|                       Petersham (4), Phillipston (18), Princeton (20), Royalston (18), Sterling (61), Templeton (93), Westminster
  29|                       (81), and Winchendon (146). The remaining 26 students were from out-of-district towns, including Ayer,
  30|                       Clinton, Lancaster, Leominster, Orange, Shirley, Webster and Worcester.
  31|                       Throughout 2014-2015, Monty Tech offered a variety of opportunities for students, parents, and community
  32|                       members to learn about and visit the school. In October 2014, approximately 1,000 district eighth graders
  33|                       participated in the annual "Tour Day" event. Students toured our twenty vocational-technical areas and
  34|                       learned about the school's challenging academic offerings and exciting athletic and extracurricular
  35|                       programs. Career Awareness Night offered interested students the opportunity to return in the evening with
  36|                       their family members, to further explore the facilities and talk with staff members.
  37|                        Each year, the Dean of Admissions conducts school visits, student interviews, and accepts applications for
  38|                       admissions. 2014-2015 proved to be an exceptionally busy year for her, as the school received 631
  39|                       applications for admission. Of those, 575 were from students hoping to enter our incoming freshman class.
  40|                                                                                                    118

===PAGE 119=== (ocr, 45 lines)
   1|                       The balance of the applications came from students hoping to enter the school as upperclassmen. Because
   2|                       there are only a limited number of students the school can accept each year, 338 freshmen and 3
   3|                       upperclassmen were admitted.
   4|                       The Vocational Interest Program (V.I.P.) offers area seventh and eighth grade students the chance to visit
   5|                       Monty Tech atter school, and participate in hands-on learning experiences across a variety of
   6|                       vocational/technical areas. The program continued to attract a large number of students during the 2014-2015
   7|                       school year, serving approximately 600 area students.
   8|                                                                                     Class of 2015 Awards
   9|                       Members of the Class of 2015 were awarded approximately $55,000 in scholarships. The Monty Tech
  10|                       Foundation generously provided $35,000 in scholarships to graduating seniors, ranging in amounts of $200
  11|                       to $2,000. The Foundation also awarded $6,000 to the Practical Nursing graduates. Once again, local and
  12|                       state organizations, as well as generous individuals, continue to recognize the ability and potential of Monty
  13|                       Tech graduates in the form of financial donations. The School Committee, administration, faculty, and
  14|                       graduates themselves, are grateful for this support.
  15|                       Articulation Agreements with local colleges also play an important role in helping reduce the cost of higher
  16|                       education. Qualified Monty Tech students are eligible to receive college credits through a number of
  17|                       articulation agreements with public and private colleges across the country. Approximately 54% of the
  18|                       graduating class of 2015 reported plans to enroll at either a 2-year college, 4-year college/university, or a
  19|                       technical/trade school upon graduation. By earning college credits while still in high school, these students
  20|                       will benefit by saving both time and money as they pursue advanced educational programs.
  21|                                                                                        Financial Report
  22|                       In an effort to develop a cost-effective budget for the fiscal year 2014-2015, a great deal of effort was put
  23|                       forth by the School Committee, administration, and staff. The final fiscal year 2014-2015 Educational Plan
  24|                       totaled $25,640,833, which represents a 3.5% increase over the 2013-2014 Educational Plan. The District's
  25|                       FY15 budget, once again, only meets the minimum spending required by Massachusetts General Law
  26|                       Chapter 70.
  27|                       The District was audited in August 2015 as part of the yearly financial audit by the accounting firm of
  28|                       Melanson, Heath and Co. from Greenfield, MA and a very good report is anticipated.
  29|                                                                                     Grants and Contracts
  30|                       Monty Tech continues to pursue grant funding on an annual basis. These funds assist in providing many
  31|                       educational and social services to the student population. For fiscal year 2015, state and federal grant
  32|                       sources provided the school with $866,668. Programs funded by these grants include: Essential Health
  33|                       Services, Social Intervention and Mediation, Improving Teacher Quality, Special Education Services and
  34|                       Program Improvement, Title I Support, Perkins Occupational Education, and Perkins Postsecondary
  35|                       Education. Using these allocation funds, the school was able to purchase a variety of instructional
  36|                       technology, equipment and supplies to enhance the learning experience across both academic and vocational
  37|                       programs.

  18|                                                                Vocational Projects in the District Communities
  19|                       Unlike students in traditional, comprehensive high schools, students at Monty Tech are asked to put their
  20|                       education into practice on a daily basis. Students across the twenty different vocational-technical education
  21|                        programs are building homes, reconstructing damaged properties, repairing service vehicles, making

  30|                                                                                 Student Support Services
  31|                        During the 2014-2015 school year, Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District provided
  32|                       special services to approximately three hundred and fifteen students - measuring progress of over two
  33|                       hundred students on Individual Education Plans (IEPs) and just under one hundred students adhering to
  34|                       individualized Section 504 plans. While the Student Support Services (SSS) Department encompasses
  35|                       special education, the department provides support and is available to all Monty Tech students.
  36|                        The department includes a full-time nursing staff that administers medications, performs state-mandated
  37|                        health screening exams, and provides, when necessary, health information to the special education team for a
  38|                       student's IEP meeting. The department benefits from a full-time school social worker who participates in
  39|                       departmental meetings and assists students who have needs concerning finances, family issues,
  40|                       homelessness, maternity, health issues, and proper food and clothing. The school is also fortunate to have on
  41|                       staff a full-time psychologist, whose role it is to evaluate all students referred for an initial evaluation or who
  42|                       require a three-year re-evaluation. In addition, we have a full-time speech language pathologist, who is
  43|                       available to assist students with disabilities, assess these students and consult with teachers. Our students
  44|                       also have access to the services of a full-time adjustment counselor and part-time school psychologist. All of
  45|                        these individuals are available for scheduled counseling sessions and mental health emergency treatment, as
  46|                        well as crisis intervention.

  32|                        Cyber Security Team, led by First Sergeant Paul Jornet and Information Technology Instructor Richard
  33|                        Duncan, once again capturing national recognition by placing first in the Air Force Association's National
  34|                        Cyber Security Competition held in Washington, DC.

  36|                       throughout the district. The corps conducted a major canned food drive, worked side-by-side with the Marine
  37|                        Corps Reserve in a national Toys 4 Tots campaign, and spent four weekends working with the local
  38|                       Salvation Army helping to raise over $26,000 for needy families. The cadets conducted their annual 10 mile
  39|                       "March-A-Thon" to support NEADS (National Education of Assistance Dogs Services) from Princeton, MA,

  42|                                                                                                    128

   1|                        cadets with individual and team development opportunities, as well as the opportunity to visit many
   2|                        historical sites.
   3|                        During the summer of 2015, our Cadet Cyber Team was again asked to support a Cyber STEM camp for the
   4|                       National Marine Corps JROTC program. The Cyber Team coordinated the 12-day camp that focused on
   5|                       defending cyber networks from attacks. The camp also offered an introduction to robotics programming
   6|                       using the VEX Robotics System. The camp was attended by 200 students, representing thirty-five states.

  11|                       opportunity to visit both campuses to explore STEM pathways.
  12|                       The Monty Tech JROTC program received an incredible honor, having been named a Marine Corps Honor
  13|                        School by the Commanding General Marine Corps Training & Education Command. Only ten percent of
  14|                        Marine Corps JROTC programs nationwide receive this recognition. The selection was based on several
  15|                       criteria, including cadet citizenship, the percentage of cadets involved in student government organizations,
  16|                       the number of cadets active in school activities and clubs, the number of community service hours for the
  17|                       unit as a whole and per cadet, the number of organizations assisted by the unit, and scholastic achievements
  18|                       including the number of academic awards and scholarships given to cadets. The units were also measured by
  19|                       participation in public affairs events, drill team competitions, rifle team competitions, physical fitness team
  20|                       competitions, and field trips.

  22|                        will now have the opportunity to make nomination recommendations to the U.S. Naval Academy, U.S. Air
  23|                       Force Academy, and the Military Academy at West Point under the Honor School Category.
  24|                                                                                    Women in Technology
  25|                        Monty Tech is one of the original members of the North Central Massachusetts Women In Technology
  26|                        Program and the 2014-2015 school year marked the school's 13 year in this innovative school-to-business
  27|                       partnership. The highly successful collaborative program continues to grow with membership including
  28|                        students from six area high schools, introducing female students to well-paying careers in business and
  29|                       technology. Participants spend two days a month working on real-world work projects under the mentorship
  30|                       of company managers at SimplexGrinnell and Tyco Safety Products in Westminster, subsidiaries of Tyco
  31|                       International, a Fortune 500 company.
  32|                       The program has been so successful in its mission of providing a proven pathway to corporate America, that
  33|                       it was recently recognized as one of the region's premier experience-based educational programs of its kind.
  34|                        Affiliation with the program, and skills acquired through participation, open doors to career opportunities not
  35|                       otherwise available to high school students. Graduates of the program are also equipped with a foundation to
  36|                       better meet the challenges of an ever-changing and demanding work force.
  37|                        Each year, graduates of the program go on to rewarding and well-paying careers, made possible by this
  38|                       unique experience.

  17|                       trends.
  18|                                                                                 Practical Nursing Program
  19|                       The Practical Nursing Program is designed to prepare graduates to practice safely, ethically and in a caring
  20|                       manner for patients who are experiencing common variations in health status in diverse health care settings. This
  21|                       mission, which is consistent with the philosophy and goals of the Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical
  22|                       School District, accomplishes the following:
  23|                             • Identifies a strong relationship between academic and vocational preparation
  24|                                   Stresses the importance of developing critical thinking skills to function safely, effectively, and
  25|                                   productively in an ever-changing technical and diverse society
  26|                                   Supports the maintenance of a positive and caring learning and practice environment
  27|                       On June 18, 2015, the Monty Tech Practical Nursing Program saw one of its largest graduating classes - forty (40)
  28|                       students - complete the Practical Nursing Program and enter the nursing profession. The class achieved an initial
  29|                       NCLEX pass rate of 88%, and just over 75% of the 2015 graduates are currently working in the North Central
  30|                       area, in various health care settings including long-term care, sub-acute care, clinics, medical offices, and prison
  31|                       health care.
  32|                       The Monty Tech Practical Nursing Program continues to develop the "LN to BSN Bridge" relationship with
  33|                       Fitchburg State University. Both institutions were awarded a grant from the Massachusetts Department of Higher
  34|                        Education, supporting the "Nurse of the Future" initiative. The grant funding will assist veterans hoping to
  35|                       transition from military to civilian healthcare fields, granting academic credits for previous military training and
  36|                       experience in related military specialties.
  37|                       In January, the program added a technology component called Shadow Health, a virtual patient-centered clinical
  38|                       experience software package. Students were asked to complete assignments at home, and were assessed
  39|                       according to their patient/student interaction and clinical practice interactions. The
  40|                                                                                                    131

===PAGE 132=== (ocr, 45 lines)
   1|                       added technology proved to be beneficial, allowing the educational program to continue despite the
   2|                       challenging weather and school closings.
   3|                        Finally, the Monty Tech PN Class of 2015 completed a meaningful community service project, adopting a
   4|                        Monty Tech family in need referred by the school's Student Support Services Department. The nursing
   5|                       students purchased holiday gifts and food for the family, making sure they were consistent with the family
   6|                       requests and needs.
   7|                                                                                          Looking Ahead
   8|                        While the Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District educational community is certainly
   9|                       proud of the achievements of our talented students, faculty, and staff, we continue to have an eye toward the
  10|                       future, always committed to improving our vocational and academic programming, strengthening key
  11|                       partnerships, and maintaining facilities that contribute to student success and achievement. As we look
  12|                       ahead, there are a number of programs and initiatives that we expect will have a positive impact on our
  13|                       school and students for years to come.
  14|                       Expand partnerships with area businesses: To support the school's popular Business Technology program,
  15|                       specifically addressing the financial elements found within the program's frameworks, school leaders began
  16|                       exploring opportunities to bring banking to Monty Tech students. In collaboration with Workers' Credit
  17|                        Union, school officials are pleased to announce a developing partnership that will result in a full-service
  18|                       branch located on the school's campus, offering students opportunities to develop authentic financial literacy
  19|                       skills and experience while still in high school. Additionally, students studying in the school's Business
  20|                       Technology program will be trained as bank tellers, effectively preparing them for entry-level jobs in
  21|                       banking institutions across North Central Massachusetts.
  22|                       Expand partnerships with area colleges and universities: Students in Monty Tech's very busy Health
  23|                       Occupations program may just be getting busier in the coming years. While the program already offered a
  24|                       number of industry-recognized credentials, school leaders began working with college partner, Mount
  25|                        Wachusett Community College, to determine if a college-level Emergency Medical Technician (EMT)
  26|                       training program could be embedded into the senior year of study. We are pleased to announce that this
  27|                       collaboration has resulted in an agreement that will effectively allow seniors to earn 8 college credits, at no
  28|                       charge, and the opportunity to sit for the certification exam in June 2016. By providing additional career
  29|                       pathways in the medical field, and access to college level coursework while still enrolled in high school,
  30|                       school administrators and teachers are confident that program graduates will not only be more qualified for
  31|                       entry level positions, they will be more apt to find an area of interest within the medical field, and continue to
  32|                       refine the technical skills they developed while at Monty Tech.
  33|                       Expand Access to Instructional Technology: A Monty Tech education is effective because efforts are made
  34|                       to continually access our programming, instructional equipment, and our educational resources. Through
  35|                       this assessment, it has become clear that while so many students have access to technology away from the
  36|                       school, many do not. It is important, then, to arm every student with the tools necessary to succeed not only
  37|                       in the workplace, but in the classroom, as well. The district is pleased to announce a large-scale technology
  38|                       initiative that began in August 2015, when every educator at Monty Tech was provided with a Chromebook
  39|                       and individualized professional development on how to best incorporate this added technology into daily
  40|                       instruction. So many teachers have embraced the concept, and continued to explore learning opportunities
  41|                       that have resulted in classroom instruction that better reflects our 21" Century school. The Monty Tech
  42|                       technology initiative continues, and in August 2016, every student at Monty Tech will also be provided with
  43|                       a Chromebook to support his/her learning, more efficiently communicate with teachers, and to promote
  44|                        collaboration among student peers.
  45|                                                                                                    132

===PAGE 133=== (ocr, 45 lines)
   1|                       Expand vocational-technical educational opportunities: As you know, Montachusett Regional Vocational
   2|                        Technical School is home to twenty vocational-technical programs, and currently serves over 1,400 students
   3|                       from eighteen cities and towns in North Central Massachusetts. We are so proud of our students and
   4|                       accomplishments, and every year we strive to provide only the best educational programs, both academic and
   5|                       vocational, to each and every student. As we review our student demographic, the regional workforce data,
   6|                       and feedback we have received from students interested in attending our school, we consider the benefits of
   7|                        adding new vocational programs. We are pleased to announce that Monty Tech is in the development stages
   8|                        of bringing a new program - our 21" program - to the school - Animal/Veterinary Science. The new
   9|                       program will respond to much-needed workforce training and community services, and will effectively
  10|                        prepare students to enter both college and career pathways upon graduation. Students and instructors,
  11|                       collaboration with program partner, Becker College, will effectively learn concepts associated with a high
  12|                       school veterinary assisting program, while running a fully-functioning veterinary clinic, designed to provide
  13|                        care for pets in low-income families. Students will have access to college level coursework, and earn
  14|                       industry-recognized credentials, so that they may either advance to related post-secondary programs, or enter
  15|                       into the workforce to fill the projected 25.32% growth in veterinary technician opportunities through 2022.
  16|                        While this program is only in its development stages, a great deal of work has already been done to assure its
  17|                       success. Student surveys have been collected, collaborative working groups have been established, and
  18|                       industry experts across North Central Massachusetts have been called upon to offer expertise to help ensure
  19|                       the innovative facility is designed with both education and service in mind, and that all equipment and
  20|                       services align with industry standards.

   1|                        ARTICLE 26. To see if the Town will vote to amend the General Bylaws of the Town by adding Section
   2|                       XXXII, entitled Architectural Preservation District, as follows:
   3|                       Section XXXII ARCHITECTURAL PRESERVATION DISTRICT
   4|                        Section 1: Purpose
   5|                        This bylaw is enacted under the Home Rule Amendment of the Massachusetts Constitution for the purposes of:
   6|                       (a) Preserving, restoring and protecting groups of historically and/or architecturally significant buildings and the
   7|                       characteristics of their neighborhoods that are important to the town's architectural, cultural, economic, political
   8|                       and/or social history;
   9|                       (b) Fostering wider public knowledge and appreciation of such neighborhoods and Contributing Properties;
  10|                       (c) Limiting the detrimental effect of alterations (substantial & minor), additions, and demolitions on the character
  11|                        of such Contributing Properties and their neighborhood settings;
  12|                       (d) Reviewing proposed alterations (substantial and minor) including demolition of or to any Contributing Property
  13|                       located within the APD, for appropriateness and compatibility with the existing buildings, setting and neighborhood
  14|                        character; and
  15|                       (e) Facilitating the protection of the APD through a regulatory review.
  16|                        To achieve these purposes, the Town of Lunenburg may designate APDs to be administered as set forth in this
  17|                        bylaw.
  18|                       Section 2: Definitions
  19|                        For the purpose of this bylaw, the terms and words listed below shall have the following meaning:
  20|                        ADDITION: Any addition to a principal or accessory Contributing Property that is enclosed by walls and which
  21|                       increases the existing gross floor area.
  22|                       ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW/DETERMINATION OF APPLICABILITY: Pursuant to Section 7 of this
  23|                       bylaw, a process to review proposed alterations to Contributing Properties and identify the need for Binding Review.
  24|                        AGGRIEVED PARTY: The owner of the subject property or an owner of real property located within the APD or
  25|                       within three hundred feet of the subject property.
  26|                       ALTERATION, MINOR: Replacement, modification or material change to existing architectural features on a
  27|                       Contributing Property, which retains the character of the property as determined by the Architectural Preservation
  28|                       District Commission. Examples include, but are not limited to windows, doors, roof material and trim work.
  29|                       ALTERATION, SUBSTANTIAL: A change to a Contributing Property or part thereof, such as removal,
  30|                       reconstruction, restoration, replication, rehabilitation, addition, or demolition; and/or a change to a site that includes,
  31|                       enlarging or moving a building and other similar activities.
  32|                       ARCHITECTURAL PRESERVATION DISTRICT ("APD"): An area of historic and /or architectural
  33|                       significance determined by the Town's residents to be worthy of preservation.
  34|                        BINDING REVIEW: Pursuant to Section 8 of this bylaw, a mandatory process which applies to substantial
  35|                       alterations of contributing properties, including demolition, in the APD.
  36|                        BUILDING: A combination of materials having a roof, the purpose of which is the shelter of persons, animals,
  37|                       property, or processes, including any other permanent structure.
  38|                        CERTIFICATE TO ALTER: A document issued by the APDC allowing Alterations pursuant to Section 8 of this
  39|                       bylaw.
  40|                       CONTRIBUTING PROPERTY: Any building or stone wall within an APD, which is older than 75 years and
  41|                       contributes to the Architectural Preservation District's historical character as determined by the Architectural
  42|                        Preservation District Commission.
  43|                                                                                                    144

===PAGE 145=== (ocr, 28 lines)
   1|                       DEMOLITION: The act of removing or razing structures or significant parts of structures, or commencing the work of total
   2|                       or substantial destruction with the intent of completing the same.
   3|                       DEMOLITION BY NEGLECT: Destruction by failure to maintain roof, siding, foundation or any other aspect that requires
   4|                       upkeep, which could ultimately result in the Contributing Property being condemned. These include but are not limited to:
   5|                             1. Facades which may fall and injure members of the public or property.
   6|                            2. Deteriorated or inadequate foundation, deteriorated flooring or floor supports, deteriorated walls or other vertical
   7|                                   structural supports.
   8|                            3. Members of ceilings, roofs, ceiling and roof supports or other horizontal members which sag, split or buckle due to
   9|                                   deterioration.
  10|                             4. Deteriorated or ineffective waterproofing of exterior walls, roof, foundations or floors, including broken windows or
  11|                                   doors.
  12|                             5. Improper or insufficient waterproofing or exterior wall covering, including lack of paint or weathering due to lack of
  13|                                   paint or other protective covering.
  14|                             6. Any fault or defect in the Contributing Property caused by alteration or neglect of maintenance, which renders it not
  15|                                   properly watertight or structurally unsafe.
  16|                             7. Fireplaces or chimneys which list, bulge or settle due to deterioration.
  17|                       DESIGN GUIDELINES: A public document which provides further detail and illustration of the design standards
  18|                       established in Section 9 of this bylaw. Such guidelines, by facilitating the APDC's determination as to whether proposed
  19|                       alterations are appropriate and compatible with the existing Contributing Property's, setting and neighborhood character of
  20|                       the APD, will ensure fair, reasonable and objective preservation practices by the APDC.
